sectionTitle: Synthetic and naturally occurring polymers (chemistry only)

specStatements.text: Alkenes can be used to make polymers such as poly(ethene) and poly(propene) by addition polymerisation.
In addition polymerisation reactions, many small molecules (monomers) join together to form very large molecules (polymers).
For example:
In addition polymers the repeating unit has the same atoms as the monomer because no other molecule is formed in the reaction.
Students should be able to:
recognise addition polymers and monomers from diagrams in the forms shown and from the presence of the functional group C=C in the monomers
draw diagrams to represent the formation of a polymer from a given alkene monomer
relate the repeating unit to the monomer.

Condensation polymerisation involves monomers with two functional groups. When these types of monomers react they join together, usually losing small molecules such as water, and so the reactions are called condensation reactions.
The simplest polymers are produced from two different monomers with two of the same functional groups on each monomer.
For example:
ethanediol
and
hexanedioic acid
polymerise to produce a polyester:
Amino acids have two different functional groups in a molecule. Amino acids react by condensation polymerisation to produce polypeptides.
For example: glycine is H₂ NCH₂ COOH and polymerises to produce the polypeptide
Different amino acids can be combined in the same chain to produce proteins.
DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) is a large molecule essential for life. DNA encodes genetic instructions for the development and functioning of living organisms and viruses.

Most DNA molecules are two polymer chains, made from four different monomers called nucleotides, in the form of a double helix. Other naturally occurring polymers important for life include proteins, starch and cellulose.
Students should be able to name the types of monomers from which these naturally occurring polymers are made.

concepts.definition: A small molecule that joins together with many others of its kind to form a polymer. In addition polymerisation the monomer must contain a carbon–carbon double bond, C=C.
A very large molecule formed when many small molecules (monomers) join together. One polymer molecule may contain thousands of monomer units joined in a chain.
A reaction in which many small unsaturated molecules (monomers) join together to form one very large molecule (a polymer). It is the only product: no other molecule is formed.
Alkenes contain the functional group C=C. This double bond can open up so that the molecule bonds to the molecules either side of it, which is why alkenes can be used to make addition polymers.
The addition polymer made from the monomer ethene, CH₂=CH₂. The equation is n CH₂=CH₂ → –(CH₂–CH₂)ₙ–, so the repeating unit is –CH₂–CH₂–.
The addition polymer made from the monomer propene, CH₃CH=CH₂. The repeating unit is –CH₂–CH(CH₃)–, which contains the same atoms as one propene molecule, C₃H₆.

The part of a polymer chain that repeats over and over. In an addition polymer it has the same atoms as the monomer, because no other molecule is formed in the reaction; the only change is that the C=C double bond has become a C–C single bond.

The monomer is drawn with its C=C double bond and n written in front of it. The polymer is drawn as the repeating unit inside brackets, with a bond passing out through each bracket to show the chain continues, and n written after the closing bracket.

The carbon–carbon double bond. Its presence in a molecule is how you recognise that the molecule can act as a monomer for addition polymerisation; its absence from the repeating unit is how you recognise the polymer.

To go from monomer to repeating unit, change the C=C to a single bond and add a bond out of each end. To go from repeating unit to monomer, remove the bonds sticking out and put the double bond back between the two carbon atoms of the unit.

Polymerisation in which monomers with two functional groups join together, usually losing small molecules such as water. The simplest condensation polymers are made from two different monomers, each carrying two of the same functional group.

A reaction in which molecules join together and a small molecule, such as water, is lost. Because polymerisation of monomers with two functional groups works this way, it is called condensation polymerisation.
The condensation polymer formed when ethanediol and hexanedioic acid polymerise. Each –OH group reacts with a –COOH group, water is lost, and an ester link joins the two monomer units.
HOCH₂CH₂OH: a monomer with two of the same functional group, an –OH group at each end of the molecule.
HOOC(CH₂)₄COOH: a monomer with two of the same functional group, a –COOH group at each end of the molecule.
n HOCH₂CH₂OH + n HOOC(CH₂)₄COOH → –(O–CH₂CH₂–O–CO–(CH₂)₄–CO)ₙ– + 2n H₂O. Each of the 2n functional groups on one monomer pairs with one on the other, so 2n water molecules are lost.
A molecule with two different functional groups: an amino group, –NH₂, and a carboxyl group, –COOH. Having two functional groups is what allows amino acids to polymerise by condensation.
The simplest amino acid, H₂NCH₂COOH. It polymerises by condensation: n H₂NCH₂COOH → –(HN–CH₂–CO)ₙ– + n H₂O.
The condensation polymer produced when amino acids react together. The –NH₂ group of one amino acid reacts with the –COOH group of the next, and a water molecule is lost each time a link is made.
A naturally occurring polymer produced when different amino acids are combined in the same chain. Amino acids are the monomers from which proteins are made.
A large molecule essential for life. DNA encodes the genetic instructions for the development and functioning of living organisms and viruses.
The monomer from which DNA is made. There are four different nucleotides, and they join into long polymer chains.
The shape of most DNA molecules: two polymer chains of nucleotides twisted around each other.
Polymers made by living things rather than in industry. As well as DNA, those important for life include proteins, starch and cellulose.
DNA is made from nucleotides; proteins are made from amino acids; starch and cellulose are both made from the sugar glucose.

misconceptions.question: Which molecule is the monomer for poly(ethene)?
misconceptions.correct: Ethene, CH₂=CH₂, which contains a C=C double bond.
misconceptions.misconception: Poly(ethene) must be made from ethane, because ethane is the ordinary hydrocarbon with two carbons and the names sound the same.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Ethene' and 'ethane' differ by one letter and sound almost identical when spoken, and alkanes are met first, so the more familiar name is recalled.
misconceptions.correction: The specification is specific: alkenes are used to make addition polymers. Ethane, C₂H₆, has only single bonds and nothing that can open up, so it cannot polymerise. Only ethene, with its C=C, can.

misconceptions.question: Can any hydrocarbon be used as a monomer for addition polymerisation?
misconceptions.correct: No. Only molecules containing the functional group C=C can undergo addition polymerisation.
misconceptions.misconception: Polymers are just long chains of carbon and hydrogen, so any hydrocarbon can join up to make one.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students see that the polymer contains only carbon and hydrogen and reason backwards that any carbon–hydrogen molecule would do.
misconceptions.correction: Joining requires a bond that can open. In an alkane every bond is already a single bond and every carbon is bonded to as many atoms as it can be, so there is nothing to open. The C=C is what makes addition polymerisation possible.

misconceptions.question: Is anything else produced when an addition polymer forms?
misconceptions.correct: No. The polymer is the only product, which is why the repeating unit has the same atoms as the monomer.
misconceptions.misconception: Water is given off when monomers join together, because a reaction that joins molecules has to squeeze something out.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Condensation polymerisation, and reactions like esterification, are met alongside this and both release water, so the idea gets attached to all polymerisation.
misconceptions.correction: In addition polymerisation the monomers simply add together: no atoms leave. That is exactly why the repeating unit contains the same atoms as the monomer.

misconceptions.question: Does the repeating unit of an addition polymer still contain a C=C double bond?
misconceptions.correct: No. The double bond has opened and become a single bond between the two carbon atoms.
misconceptions.misconception: The repeating unit has the same atoms as the monomer, so it must be the same molecule, double bond and all.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Same atoms' is over-read as 'identical structure', and the double bond is the most memorable feature of the monomer, so it gets copied straight into the polymer.
misconceptions.correction: Same atoms does not mean same bonding. The C=C opens up so that each carbon can form a bond to the unit next door; drawing a double bond inside the brackets is one of the commonest ways to lose the mark.

misconceptions.question: If a repeating unit has the same atoms as the monomer, does the polymer have the same formula as the monomer?
misconceptions.correct: No. The polymer contains n repeating units, so it is thousands of times larger than one monomer molecule.
misconceptions.misconception: Poly(ethene) has the formula C₂H₄, the same as ethene, since nothing is added and nothing is lost.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The rule 'the repeating unit has the same atoms as the monomer' is remembered without the word 'unit', so it is applied to the whole molecule.
misconceptions.correction: One repeating unit has the same atoms as one monomer. The polymer molecule is made of n of those units joined together, so it is a very large molecule; that is what the n outside the bracket is telling you.

misconceptions.question: What makes a molecule able to act as a monomer?
misconceptions.correct: For addition polymerisation, the presence of the functional group C=C.
misconceptions.misconception: A monomer just has to be a small molecule, so any small molecule can polymerise.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The definition is learned as 'monomers are small molecules that join to form polymers', and the small size is taken to be the qualifying feature.
misconceptions.correction: Small size is a description, not a cause. The specification asks you to recognise monomers from the presence of the functional group C=C: no C=C, no addition polymerisation, however small the molecule.

misconceptions.question: Do the bonds passing out through the brackets have to be drawn?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. They show that the repeating unit is bonded to the units on either side of it in the chain.
misconceptions.misconception: Those two little bonds are just decoration, so leaving them off does not really matter.
misconceptions.whyItArises: They lead to nothing visible on the page, so they look like unfinished drawing rather than chemistry.
misconceptions.correction: They carry meaning: they say the chain continues in both directions. Without them the diagram shows a separate small molecule, not part of a polymer, and the mark is not awarded.

misconceptions.question: What does the letter n mean in a polymer equation?
misconceptions.correct: It stands for a very large number of monomer molecules, and the same number of repeating units in the polymer.
misconceptions.misconception: The n tells you how many carbon atoms are in the chain.
misconceptions.whyItArises: n is used for counts elsewhere in chemistry, including in the general formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ where it does count carbon atoms, so the meaning is carried over.
misconceptions.correction: In a polymer equation n counts monomer molecules, not atoms. n monomer molecules give a chain of n repeating units, which is why n appears in front of the monomer and after the bracket.

misconceptions.question: How many kinds of monomer take part in an addition polymerisation?
misconceptions.correct: One. Many molecules of the same alkene monomer join together.
misconceptions.misconception: Addition polymerisation means adding one monomer to a different monomer, so two different monomers alternate along the chain.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word 'addition' suggests adding one thing to another thing, and condensation polymerisation, which does use two different monomers, is taught nearby.
misconceptions.correction: In addition polymerisation the monomers add to each other: many molecules of the same alkene. It is condensation polymerisation whose simplest examples use two different monomers.

misconceptions.question: When the C=C opens up, do the carbon atoms gain any hydrogen atoms?
misconceptions.correct: No. Each carbon uses the freed bond to join to the next unit in the chain, so the atoms are unchanged.
misconceptions.misconception: Turning a double bond into a single bond leaves the carbons short of a bond, so they must pick up hydrogen atoms; a C₄H₈ monomer therefore gives a C₄H₁₀ unit.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students remember alkenes reacting with hydrogen, and the idea of 'filling up' the freed bonds with hydrogen is carried into polymerisation.
misconceptions.correction: The freed bonds are used to join to the neighbouring repeating units, not to hydrogen. Nothing is added, so the repeating unit of poly(butene) is C₄H₈, exactly the atoms of the monomer.

misconceptions.question: Is a group such as –OH or a chlorine atom enough to make a molecule an addition monomer?
misconceptions.correct: No. For addition polymerisation the monomer must contain C=C.
misconceptions.misconception: Any reactive-looking group will do, because a monomer just needs somewhere reactive for the joining to happen.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Functional group' is learned as a general idea about reactivity, so any functional group is treated as equally able to make a polymer.
misconceptions.correction: The specification names the group: monomers are recognised from the presence of the functional group C=C. Molecules such as ethanol or dichloroethane have no C=C and do not undergo addition polymerisation.

misconceptions.question: In a condensation reaction, is water added or lost?
misconceptions.correct: Lost. The monomers join together and small molecules such as water are released.
misconceptions.misconception: Condensation means water appearing, so water must be added to the monomers to stick them together.
misconceptions.whyItArises: In everyday life condensation is water appearing on a cold window, so the word is associated with water arriving rather than with molecules joining.
misconceptions.correction: In chemistry a condensation reaction is one where molecules join and a small molecule is released. The water appears as a separate product, released by the monomers, not consumed by them.

misconceptions.question: Do condensation monomers need a C=C double bond?
misconceptions.correct: No. They need two functional groups, such as two –OH groups or two –COOH groups.
misconceptions.misconception: All polymerisation works by a double bond opening up, so condensation monomers must contain C=C as well.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Addition polymerisation is taught first and its C=C rule is strong and memorable, so it is generalised to every polymerisation.
misconceptions.correction: Condensation polymerisation is a different mechanism. Ethanediol and hexanedioic acid contain no C=C at all; what they have is two functional groups each, which is what lets a chain build up in both directions.

misconceptions.question: Why is condensation polymerisation called condensation?
misconceptions.correct: Because as the monomers join, small molecules such as water are lost, and that is what a condensation reaction is.
misconceptions.misconception: The mixture is cooled until the vapour condenses into a liquid, and that liquid is the polymer.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Condensation has been met in distillation and fractional distillation as a change of state, so the same physical meaning is imported.
misconceptions.correction: Here the word describes a type of reaction, not a change of state. No condensing of vapour is involved: monomers bond together and expel a small molecule.

misconceptions.question: In the simplest condensation polymers, how are the functional groups arranged on each monomer?
misconceptions.correct: Each monomer carries two of the same functional group, and the two monomers are different from each other.
misconceptions.misconception: Each monomer has two different functional groups, one at each end.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Two functional groups' and 'two different monomers' both appear in the same sentence, and the word 'different' gets attached to the wrong noun.
misconceptions.correction: Read the statement carefully: two different monomers, with two of the same functional groups on each monomer. Ethanediol has two –OH groups; hexanedioic acid has two –COOH groups. It is amino acids that carry two different groups in one molecule.

misconceptions.question: Could ethanol and ethanoic acid make a condensation polymer?
misconceptions.correct: No. Each has only one functional group, so the chain cannot grow at both ends.
misconceptions.misconception: One functional group on each monomer is enough, because that is all you need for the two molecules to react.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students have seen an alcohol react with an acid to make a single ester, and assume that repeating the same reaction automatically builds a polymer.
misconceptions.correction: Two molecules with one group each react once and stop: the product has no groups left to continue. A polymer needs each monomer to have two functional groups so that every unit can bond on both sides.

misconceptions.question: Which functional groups are on ethanediol and which are on hexanedioic acid?
misconceptions.correct: Ethanediol has two –OH groups; hexanedioic acid has two –COOH groups.
misconceptions.misconception: Ethanediol is the one with the –COOH groups, because it comes first in the equation and looks like the more complicated molecule.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both formulae begin with the letters HO, so they look alike at a glance and the names are not read for their meaning.
misconceptions.correction: Read the names: 'ethane-di-ol' means two alcohol (–OH) groups; 'hexane-di-oic acid' means two carboxylic acid (–COOH) groups. The formulae confirm it: HOCH₂CH₂OH and HOOC(CH₂)₄COOH.

misconceptions.question: How many water molecules form when n ethanediol react with n hexanedioic acid?
misconceptions.correct: 2n, because each monomer contributes two functional groups and each link made releases one water molecule.
misconceptions.misconception: One water molecule is lost per pair of monomers, so n pairs give n water molecules.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The single ester reaction, alcohol plus acid giving one water, is remembered and applied to the whole polymerisation without counting the links.
misconceptions.correction: Each monomer joins at both ends, so n + n monomers make 2n links along the chain and 2n water molecules are released. The balanced equation shows 2n H₂O.

misconceptions.question: Is the polymer the only product of a condensation polymerisation?
misconceptions.correct: No. Small molecules such as water are also produced.
misconceptions.misconception: Polymerisation makes a polymer, so the polymer is the only thing on the right-hand side of the equation.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Addition polymerisation is learned first and genuinely has one product, so the same pattern is expected for condensation.
misconceptions.correction: That single-product rule belongs to addition polymerisation only. In condensation polymerisation the small molecule lost must appear in the equation, otherwise it does not balance.

misconceptions.question: What small molecule is lost when a polyester forms?
misconceptions.correct: Water.
misconceptions.misconception: Carbon dioxide is given off, because the monomer is an acid and acids release carbon dioxide.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Carboxylic acids are strongly associated with the carbonate reaction that fizzes and releases carbon dioxide, so any reaction of a –COOH group is expected to do the same.
misconceptions.correction: No carbonate is present here. The –OH of one monomer and the –COOH of the other combine, and the atoms removed make H₂O. The carbon stays in the polymer chain.

misconceptions.question: How many different functional groups does one amino acid molecule contain?
misconceptions.correct: Two different ones: an amino group, –NH₂, and a carboxyl group, –COOH.
misconceptions.misconception: Amino acids must carry two of the same group at each end, just like ethanediol and hexanedioic acid do.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The rule from the polyester example, 'two of the same functional groups on each monomer', is remembered as the rule for all condensation monomers.
misconceptions.correction: The specification draws the contrast deliberately: amino acids have two different functional groups in a molecule. That is why one amino acid can polymerise with itself, whereas a polyester needs two different monomers.

misconceptions.question: By what type of polymerisation do amino acids react?
misconceptions.correct: Condensation polymerisation, producing polypeptides and losing water.
misconceptions.misconception: Amino acids contain a C=O double bond, so they must polymerise by addition, with the double bond opening up.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The rule 'double bond means addition polymerisation' is remembered as being about any double bond, rather than about the C=C group specifically.
misconceptions.correction: Only C=C opens up in addition polymerisation. The C=O in the –COOH group stays intact; amino acids join through their –NH₂ and –COOH groups, losing water, which is condensation polymerisation.

misconceptions.question: What is the polymer made from amino acids called?
misconceptions.correct: A polypeptide.
misconceptions.misconception: Amino acids contain a –COOH group, so the polymer they make is a polyester.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The polyester example immediately before this one uses a –COOH monomer, so the group becomes attached to the product name.
misconceptions.correction: The link formed depends on both groups involved. In a polyester a –COOH reacts with an –OH; in a polypeptide a –COOH reacts with an –NH₂, and the product is a polypeptide, not a polyester.

misconceptions.question: What happens to the –COOH group of glycine when it polymerises?
misconceptions.correct: The –OH part is lost as water; the remaining –CO– becomes part of the chain.
misconceptions.misconception: The whole –COOH group is kept in the polymer, and only a hydrogen atom is lost from the –NH₂ end.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students know that a water molecule is lost and account for it by taking a hydrogen from one end and, wrongly, leaving the rest untouched, forgetting that water needs an oxygen too.
misconceptions.correction: Water is H₂O: an H from the –NH₂ of one molecule and an OH from the –COOH of the next. So the repeating unit is –HN–CH₂–CO–, and the equation is n H₂NCH₂COOH → –(HN–CH₂–CO)ₙ– + n H₂O.

misconceptions.question: What makes a chain of amino acids a protein?
misconceptions.correct: Different amino acids combined in the same chain.
misconceptions.misconception: A protein is just a long polypeptide, so a chain made of one amino acid over and over counts as a protein once it is long enough.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Protein' and 'polypeptide' are used loosely as synonyms in everyday teaching, and length feels like the obvious difference.
misconceptions.correction: The specification is precise: different amino acids can be combined in the same chain to produce proteins. It is the variety of amino acids, not the length of the chain, that is being described here.

misconceptions.question: What is DNA for?
misconceptions.correct: It encodes the genetic instructions for the development and functioning of living organisms and viruses.
misconceptions.misconception: DNA is a natural polymer that stores energy for the cell, in the way starch does in a plant.
misconceptions.whyItArises: DNA is listed alongside starch and cellulose as natural polymers, so the role of one is spread across the group.
misconceptions.correction: The natural polymers listed together do different jobs. DNA's job is to carry genetic instructions; storing energy is what starch does.

misconceptions.question: Which things carry genetic instructions in DNA?
misconceptions.correct: Living organisms and viruses.
misconceptions.misconception: Only living organisms use DNA, because viruses are not alive.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students are taught that viruses are not living things, and conclude that they cannot have the molecule described as essential for life.
misconceptions.correction: The specification names both: DNA encodes genetic instructions for the development and functioning of living organisms and viruses. Being non-living does not stop a virus carrying genetic material.

misconceptions.question: What are the monomers of DNA?
misconceptions.correct: Four different monomers called nucleotides.
misconceptions.misconception: DNA is made from amino acids, because amino acids are the building blocks you hear about in biology.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Amino acids are the most familiar biological monomer, and DNA and protein are discussed together in genetics, so the monomers get swapped.
misconceptions.correction: Keep the pairings separate: proteins are made from amino acids, DNA is made from nucleotides, and starch and cellulose are made from glucose.

misconceptions.question: How many different monomers make up DNA?
misconceptions.correct: Four different nucleotides.
misconceptions.misconception: DNA has two chains, so it must be built from two different monomers, one for each chain.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Two separate numbers, two chains and four monomers, sit in the same sentence, and the more visual one takes over.
misconceptions.correction: The two numbers describe different things. Most DNA molecules are two polymer chains, and those chains are made from four different monomers called nucleotides.

misconceptions.question: What is the shape of most DNA molecules?
misconceptions.correct: Two polymer chains in the form of a double helix.
misconceptions.misconception: DNA is one long chain twisted into a spiral, and the word double refers to that spiral shape.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The image of a twisted spiral is remembered from pictures, and 'double' is read as describing the twist rather than the number of chains.
misconceptions.correction: Double refers to the number of chains: most DNA molecules are two polymer chains wound into a double helix.

misconceptions.question: What monomer is cellulose made from?
misconceptions.correct: Glucose.
misconceptions.misconception: Cellulose is made from cellulase, because the names are so close.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Cellulase, the enzyme, is met in biology and the two words are almost identical, so one is substituted for the other.
misconceptions.correction: Cellulase is an enzyme that breaks cellulose down; it is not a monomer. Both starch and cellulose are polymers of the sugar glucose.

misconceptions.question: Are all naturally occurring polymers made from the same kind of monomer?
misconceptions.correct: No. DNA is made from nucleotides, proteins from amino acids, starch and cellulose from glucose.
misconceptions.misconception: Natural polymers are all built from the same sort of building block, so one answer works for all of them.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The polymers are listed together in one sentence, which makes them look like one category with one shared answer.
misconceptions.correction: Being natural polymers is all they have in common. You are asked to name the type of monomer for each: nucleotides for DNA, amino acids for proteins, glucose for starch and for cellulose.

misconceptions.question: What is the repeating unit of poly(propene)?
misconceptions.correct: –CH₂–CH(CH₃)–, containing the same atoms as one propene molecule.
misconceptions.misconception: Poly(propene) has three carbons in a row in its backbone, so the repeating unit is –CH₂–CH₂–CH₂–.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Propene has three carbon atoms, so students draw all three into the chain, forgetting that only the two carbons of the C=C join into the backbone.
misconceptions.correction: Only the two carbon atoms of the double bond become part of the backbone. The third carbon stays as a –CH₃ branch, giving –CH₂–CH(CH₃)–; the atom count, C₃H₆, is still the same as the monomer.

misconceptions.question: What does a structure drawn inside brackets with a subscript n represent?
misconceptions.correct: The repeating unit of a polymer, with the bonds through the brackets showing that the chain continues.
misconceptions.misconception: It is a small molecule, so it must be the monomer being shown before it reacts.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The unit inside the brackets is drawn at the same size as a monomer, and its small size is taken as the clue rather than the brackets and the n.
misconceptions.correction: The brackets, the n and the bonds passing through the brackets all mark it as a polymer. A monomer is drawn with no brackets, no n, and with its C=C double bond in place.

misconceptions.question: Does every functional group release its own separate water molecule?
misconceptions.correct: No. One water molecule is released each time two functional groups react together to form a link.
misconceptions.misconception: Each monomer pair has four functional groups altogether, so four water molecules must come off each time.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students count functional groups rather than links, and each group looks as though it must lose something of its own.
misconceptions.correction: Water is formed from two groups at once, an –OH and a –COOH, so the count follows the number of links, not the number of groups: n and n monomers give 2n links and 2n water molecules.

mcqs.stem: Poly(ethene) and poly(propene) are made by addition polymerisation. Which type of compound is used as the monomer, and why?

options.text: Alkanes, because their molecules are saturated hydrocarbons
options.rationale: Saturated sounds stable and complete, which some students read as ready to be joined into long chains.

options.text: Alkenes, because their molecules contain a C=C double bond
options.rationale: The specification states that alkenes can be used to make polymers by addition polymerisation; the C=C is the group that opens to form the chain.

options.text: Alkanes such as ethane, which the polymer is named after
options.rationale: Poly(ethene) and ethane sound almost the same, so the more familiar alkane name is chosen.

options.text: Any hydrocarbon, because polymers are long carbon chains
options.rationale: The product contains only carbon and hydrogen, so students reason that any hydrocarbon could have made it.

mcqs.stem: Propene, CH₃CH=CH₂, undergoes addition polymerisation. Which name and repeating unit are both correct?

options.text: Poly(propene), with the repeating unit –CH₂–CH(CH₃)–
options.rationale: The polymer keeps the monomer's name in brackets, and only the two carbons of the C=C enter the backbone, leaving a –CH₃ branch.

options.text: Poly(propane), because the C=C has become a single bond
options.rationale: The disappearance of the double bond is taken to mean the polymer should now be named after the alkane.

options.text: Poly(propene), with a repeating unit of –CH₂–CH₂–CH₂–
options.rationale: All three carbons of propene are drawn into the backbone, losing the methyl branch.

options.text: Poly(propene), with a repeating unit of –CH₂=CH(CH₃)–
options.rationale: The double bond is carried straight into the repeating unit because the atoms are unchanged.

mcqs.stem: What happens in an addition polymerisation reaction?

options.text: One very large molecule breaks down into many small monomers
options.rationale: The direction of the reaction is reversed; students who picture polymer chains being cut up choose this.

options.text: Two different monomers join together in an alternating chain
options.rationale: 'Addition' is read as adding one substance to a different substance.

options.text: Many small monomer molecules join, releasing water molecules
options.rationale: Water is expected as a by-product because joining reactions elsewhere release it.

options.text: Many small monomer molecules join to form very large molecules
options.rationale: This is the specification's definition: many small molecules (monomers) join together to form very large molecules (polymers).

mcqs.stem: 6000 ethene molecules, C₂H₄, join together in an addition polymerisation. Which statement about the polymer molecule formed is correct?

options.text: It contains 6000 repeating units and 6000 water molecules
options.rationale: The unit count is right, but water is wrongly expected as a second product.

options.text: It contains 3000 repeating units, as monomers join in pairs
options.rationale: Students who picture monomers pairing up first then halve the number of units.

options.text: It contains 6000 repeating units, each with the atoms C₂H₄
options.rationale: n monomer molecules give n repeating units, and each unit has the same atoms as the monomer because nothing else is formed.

options.text: It has the formula C₂H₄, the same as the monomer molecule
options.rationale: 'Same atoms as the monomer' is applied to the whole polymer rather than to one repeating unit.

mcqs.stem: Which equation correctly represents the addition polymerisation of ethene?

options.text: n CH₂=CH₂ → –(CH₂–CH₂)ₙ–
options.rationale: The monomer has its C=C, the repeating unit has a single bond and bonds through the brackets, and n appears on both sides.

options.text: n CH₃–CH₃ → –(CH₂–CH₂)ₙ–
options.rationale: Ethane is written as the monomer because its name is so close to ethene.

options.text: n CH₂=CH₂ → –(CH₂=CH₂)ₙ–
options.rationale: The double bond is kept inside the brackets, since the atoms do not change.

options.text: n CH₂=CH₂ → –(CH₂–CH₂)–
options.rationale: The subscript n is dropped because it is thought to be optional labelling.

mcqs.stem: Why does the repeating unit of an addition polymer contain exactly the same atoms as its monomer?

options.text: The double bond of the monomer is kept in the repeating unit
options.rationale: Sameness of atoms is explained by sameness of bonding, which is the wrong reason.

options.text: No other molecule is formed in the reaction, so no atoms leave
options.rationale: This is the reason the specification gives: the polymer is the only product, so every atom of the monomer is still there.

options.text: A water molecule is lost, but water is not counted as a product
options.rationale: Water is assumed to be released and then explained away so the atoms still match.

options.text: The monomers are simply mixed together rather than reacting
options.rationale: Students who think no reaction occurs conclude that nothing about the atoms can change.

mcqs.stem: Butene, C₄H₈, undergoes addition polymerisation. What is the formula of the repeating unit of the polymer formed?

options.text: C₄H₆, because two hydrogen atoms are lost as the chain forms
options.rationale: Something is expected to be given off, and hydrogen is the easiest atom to imagine leaving.

options.text: C₄H₁₀, because the double bond changes to a single bond
options.rationale: The freed bonds are thought to be filled by extra hydrogen atoms.

options.text: C₈H₁₆, because two monomers join to make one repeating unit
options.rationale: The repeating unit is taken to be the smallest piece of chain containing a join, so it is doubled.

options.text: C₄H₈, since the repeating unit has the same atoms as the monomer
options.rationale: No other molecule is formed, so the unit contains exactly the atoms of one butene molecule.

mcqs.stem: Which molecule could act as a monomer for addition polymerisation?

options.text: CH₃–CH₂–CH₃, which is a small hydrocarbon molecule
options.rationale: Being a small hydrocarbon is taken to be what qualifies a molecule as a monomer.

options.text: CH₃–CH₂–OH, which contains a reactive –OH group
options.rationale: Any functional group is assumed to be enough for polymerisation to happen.

options.text: CH₂Cl–CH₂Cl, which has two reactive chlorine atoms
options.rationale: Halogen atoms look reactive, and having two of them suggests joining at both ends.

options.text: CH₂=CH–CH₃, which contains a C=C functional group
options.rationale: The specification asks students to recognise monomers from the presence of the functional group C=C, which this molecule has.

mcqs.stem: A structure is drawn inside square brackets, with a bond passing out through each bracket and a subscript n. What does this structure represent?

options.text: The repeating unit of a polymer, and where the chain continues
options.rationale: Brackets with bonds passing through them and a subscript n are the conventional way of showing a repeating unit within a chain.

options.text: A single monomer molecule, before any polymerisation happens
options.rationale: The unit is drawn small, so its size is read as the clue rather than the brackets and the n.

options.text: n separate monomer molecules that have not yet joined together
options.rationale: The n is read as a count of unreacted molecules, as it is on the left of the equation.

options.text: The whole polymer molecule, which is exactly n atoms long
options.rationale: n is misread as a number of atoms rather than a number of repeating units.

mcqs.stem: A student draws poly(ethene) as –CH₂–CH₂– inside brackets with a subscript n, but leaves out the bonds that pass through the brackets. Which comment on the diagram is correct?

options.text: Nothing is wrong, because those two bonds are optional here
options.rationale: The bonds lead nowhere on the page, so they look like decoration rather than chemistry.

options.text: The bonds are needed to show the unit joins to units either side
options.rationale: The extended bonds are what show that this unit is part of a continuing chain rather than a separate small molecule.

options.text: Without them, the water molecule produced cannot be shown
options.rationale: A second product is expected, and the missing bonds are assumed to be where it belongs.

options.text: The brackets should hold the monomer, not the repeating unit
options.rationale: Monomer and repeating unit are confused because they contain the same atoms.

mcqs.stem: In the equation for the formation of poly(ethene), the letter n appears in front of the monomer and as a subscript after the brackets. What does n stand for?

options.text: The number of carbon atoms in the finished polymer chain
options.rationale: n counts carbon atoms in the general formula of the alkanes, so the meaning is carried over.

options.text: The number of water molecules lost as the monomers join
options.rationale: Water is expected as a product, so the n is read as counting it.

options.text: The number of times the mixture must be heated with a catalyst
options.rationale: n is treated as a condition of the reaction rather than as a count of particles.

options.text: A large number of monomers, giving that many repeating units
options.rationale: n monomer molecules join to give a chain of n repeating units, which is why the same n appears on both sides.

mcqs.stem: The repeating unit of an addition polymer is –CH₂–CH(CH₃)–. What was the monomer?

options.text: CH₃–CH₂–CH₃, since the unit contains only single bonds
options.rationale: The repeating unit is copied straight back as the monomer, with hydrogens added to fill the free bonds.

options.text: CH₂=CH–CH₂–CH₃, since a carbon is hidden in the brackets
options.rationale: The branch is miscounted as an extra carbon in the chain, giving a four-carbon monomer.

options.text: CH₂=CH–CH₃, since the single bond in the unit was a C=C
options.rationale: To reverse the polymerisation, remove the bonds through the brackets and put the double bond back between the two backbone carbons.

options.text: CH₂=CH₂ and CH₄, since two monomers formed this unit
options.rationale: The unit is split into two pieces because addition is thought to involve two different monomers.

mcqs.stem: Poly(ethene) and poly(propene) are both addition polymers. Which comparison of a repeating unit with its monomer is correct?

options.text: Exactly the same atoms, and the C=C double bond is retained
options.rationale: 'Same atoms' is over-read as 'identical structure', keeping the double bond.

options.text: Two fewer hydrogens, which are lost as hydrogen gas forms
options.rationale: A small molecule is expected to be given off whenever monomers join.

options.text: The same atoms, but the C=C has become a C–C single bond
options.rationale: No other molecule is formed, so the atoms are unchanged; the double bond opens so each carbon can bond to the next unit.

options.text: Twice as many atoms, as monomers pair up before they join
options.rationale: The repeating unit is imagined as the pair of monomers that made the first link.

mcqs.stem: What happens in a condensation polymerisation reaction?

options.text: Monomers containing C=C join without any molecules being lost
options.rationale: The rules for addition polymerisation are applied to condensation as well.

options.text: Small molecules such as water are added across the polymer
options.rationale: Condensation is read as water appearing on, rather than leaving, the molecules.

options.text: Monomers with two functional groups join, usually losing water
options.rationale: This is the specification's description: monomers with two functional groups react and small molecules such as water are lost.

options.text: A polymer chain is broken down by water into its monomers
options.rationale: Water is known to be involved somewhere, so the reaction is imagined running the other way.

mcqs.stem: Why are the reactions that form polyesters and polypeptides called condensation reactions?

options.text: Because water is added to the monomers to make them join up
options.rationale: Everyday condensation is water arriving, so water is assumed to be a reactant.

options.text: Because small molecules such as water are lost as monomers join
options.rationale: A condensation reaction is one in which molecules join together and a small molecule is released.

options.text: Because the monomers are cooled until they condense to liquid
options.rationale: Condensation is imported from distillation as a change of state.

options.text: Because the polymer formed is much denser than the monomers
options.rationale: 'Condense' is read as becoming more compact, which fits a long packed chain.

mcqs.stem: The simplest condensation polymers are produced from two different monomers. How are the functional groups arranged?

options.text: Each monomer has two different functional groups
options.rationale: The word 'different' is attached to the groups instead of to the monomers.

options.text: Each monomer has two of the same functional group
options.rationale: The specification states that the two different monomers each carry two of the same functional groups.

options.text: Each monomer has one functional group at one end
options.rationale: One group per molecule is thought to be enough, as it is for making a single ester.

options.text: Both monomers have the same two functional groups
options.rationale: 'Two of the same functional groups' is read as the two monomers being alike.

mcqs.stem: Which pair of monomers polymerises to produce a polyester?

options.text: Ethanol, with one –OH group, and hexanoic acid
options.rationale: Monomers with a single functional group each are chosen because they still make an ester.

options.text: Ethene and hexene, which both contain a C=C bond
options.rationale: A double bond is assumed to be needed for any polymerisation.

options.text: Glycine and ethanediol, which have different groups
options.rationale: Any two monomers with different functional groups are assumed to work together.

options.text: Ethanediol, with two –OH groups, and hexanedioic acid
options.rationale: These are the two monomers named in the specification; each has two of the same functional group.

mcqs.stem: Ethanediol is HOCH₂CH₂OH and hexanedioic acid is HOOC(CH₂)₄COOH. Which statement about their functional groups is correct?

options.text: Ethanediol has two –COOH groups; the acid has two –OH groups
options.rationale: Both formulae begin with HO, so which molecule holds which group is swapped.

options.text: Each molecule has one –OH group and one –COOH group
options.rationale: The amino acid pattern of two different groups per molecule is applied here.

options.text: Ethanediol has two –OH groups; the acid has two –COOH groups
options.rationale: The names say so: 'di-ol' means two –OH groups, and 'di-oic acid' means two –COOH groups.

options.text: Both molecules contain a C=C group as well as an –OH group
options.rationale: A C=C is assumed to be present in every monomer.

mcqs.stem: n molecules of ethanediol react with n molecules of hexanedioic acid to form a polyester. How many water molecules are produced?

options.text: n
options.rationale: One water is counted per pair of monomers, as in making a single ester.

options.text: 4n
options.rationale: The four functional groups on each pair of monomers are each given their own water molecule.
The 'one fewer link than units' idea is applied, but the polymer equation is written per repeating unit.

options.text: 2n
options.rationale: Each monomer reacts at both ends, so 2n links form and 2n water molecules are released.

mcqs.stem: Ethanediol and hexanedioic acid polymerise together. What are the products of this reaction?

options.text: A polyester only, with no other product formed
options.rationale: The single-product rule of addition polymerisation is applied to condensation.

options.text: A polyester, together with carbon dioxide gas
options.rationale: A carboxylic acid is expected to give off carbon dioxide, as it does with carbonates.

options.text: A polyester, together with water molecules
options.rationale: The monomers join through their functional groups and a small molecule, water, is lost each time a link forms.

options.text: A polyester, together with hydrogen molecules
options.rationale: Something small is known to be lost, and hydrogen is the smallest molecule students think of.

mcqs.stem: Amino acids undergo condensation polymerisation. Which functional groups does one amino acid molecule contain?

options.text: One –NH₂ group and one –COOH group, which differ
options.rationale: The specification states that amino acids have two different functional groups in a molecule.

options.text: Two –COOH groups, one at each end, like a diacid
options.rationale: The polyester rule of two of the same group per monomer is applied to amino acids.

options.text: Two –NH₂ groups, one at each end of the molecule
options.rationale: The name 'amino acid' is read as being about the amino group alone, so it is doubled up.

options.text: One –OH group and one C=C group in one molecule
options.rationale: A C=C is assumed to be needed before any polymerisation can happen.

mcqs.stem: Amino acids react together to form a polymer. What is produced, and what else happens?

options.text: A polyester, because a –COOH group reacts
options.rationale: The –COOH group is associated with the polyester example met just before.

options.text: An addition polymer, since C=O bonds open up
options.rationale: Any double bond is assumed to open in the way a C=C does.

options.text: A polypeptide, with no other product formed
options.rationale: The product is right, but the small molecule lost is forgotten.

options.text: A polypeptide, and water molecules are lost
options.rationale: Amino acids react by condensation polymerisation to produce polypeptides, losing water as each link forms.

mcqs.stem: Glycine, H₂NCH₂COOH, polymerises to produce a polypeptide. Which repeating unit and other product are correct?

options.text: Repeating unit –HN–CH₂–COOH, with water also formed
options.rationale: Only a hydrogen is taken from the amino end, leaving the whole –COOH group in the chain.

options.text: Repeating unit –HN–CH₂–CO–, with water also formed
options.rationale: An H from the –NH₂ and an –OH from the –COOH are removed as water, leaving –HN–CH₂–CO– as the unit.

options.text: Repeating unit –H₂N–CH₂–CO–, with no other product formed
options.rationale: The polymer is treated as the only product, so no atoms are removed from the –NH₂ group.

options.text: Repeating unit –HN–CH₂–CO–, with hydrogen also formed
options.rationale: The unit is right, but the small molecule lost is taken to be hydrogen rather than water.

mcqs.stem: A polypeptide is made using glycine only. How would a protein differ from it?

options.text: Different amino acids would be combined in the same chain
options.rationale: The specification states that different amino acids can be combined in the same chain to produce proteins.

options.text: The chain would be made from nucleotides, not amino acids
options.rationale: The monomers of DNA and of protein are exchanged for one another.

options.text: The monomers would join by addition, not by condensation
options.rationale: A different product is assumed to require a different type of polymerisation.

options.text: Two chains would be twisted together into a double helix
options.rationale: The double helix, which belongs to DNA, is borrowed as the mark of a protein.

mcqs.stem: What does DNA do?

options.text: It stores energy for the cell to use as it develops
options.rationale: DNA is listed with starch as a natural polymer, so starch's role is transferred to it.

options.text: It carries genetic instructions in organisms but not viruses
options.rationale: Viruses are known to be non-living, so they are assumed not to have DNA.

options.text: It builds the cell walls that give living cells their shape
options.rationale: A structural role is assumed for a large molecule described as essential for life.

options.text: It encodes genetic instructions for development and functioning
options.rationale: This is the specification's wording: DNA encodes genetic instructions for the development and functioning of living organisms and viruses.

mcqs.stem: DNA is a naturally occurring polymer. What are its monomers called, and how many kinds are there?

options.text: Nucleotides, of which there are four different ones
options.rationale: The specification states that DNA is made from four different monomers called nucleotides.

options.text: Amino acids, of which there are four different ones
options.rationale: Amino acids are the most familiar biological monomer, so they are used for DNA too.

options.text: Nucleotides, of which there are two different ones
options.rationale: The two chains of the double helix are read as two kinds of monomer.

options.text: Glucose molecules, joined into two very long chains
options.rationale: One monomer is assumed to serve all the naturally occurring polymers.

mcqs.stem: Which statement describes the structure of most DNA molecules?

options.text: One polymer chain coiled up into a single helix
options.rationale: 'Double' is read as describing the twist rather than the number of chains.

options.text: Two polymer chains in the form of a double helix
options.rationale: This is the specification's description of most DNA molecules.

options.text: Four polymer chains, one for each nucleotide
options.rationale: The number of monomer types is used as the number of chains.

options.text: Two chains of amino acids wound round a core
options.rationale: The shape is right but protein monomers are substituted for nucleotides.

mcqs.stem: Starch and cellulose are naturally occurring polymers. What type of monomer is each made from?

options.text: Both are made from sugar molecules called glucose
options.rationale: Starch and cellulose are both polymers of glucose, which is the monomer students are asked to name.

options.text: Starch from glucose, and cellulose from cellulase
options.rationale: Cellulase, the enzyme met in biology, is almost the same word as cellulose.

options.text: Both are made from amino acids, as proteins are
options.rationale: One monomer is assumed to serve every naturally occurring polymer.

options.text: Starch from glucose, and cellulose from starch
options.rationale: Cellulose is treated as being built from starch because both are plant materials.

mcqs.stem: Which pairing of a naturally occurring polymer with its monomer is correct?

options.text: Proteins from nucleotides, and DNA made from amino acids
options.rationale: The two biological monomers are swapped over.

options.text: Proteins from glucose, and cellulose from amino acids
options.rationale: Monomer names are treated as interchangeable across the natural polymers.

options.text: Proteins from amino acids, and DNA from nucleotides
options.rationale: These are the monomer types the specification expects students to name for these polymers.

options.text: Proteins from amino acids, and starch from nucleotides
options.rationale: The first pairing is right, so the second is not checked carefully.
